zh:
【国风·召南】

鹊巢

维鹊有巢，维鸠居之。之子于归，百两御之。
维鹊有巢，维鸠方之。之子于归，百两将之。
维鹊有巢，维鸠盈之。之子于归，百两成之。

采蘩

于以采蘩？于沼于沚。于以用之？公侯之事。
于以采蘩，于涧之中。于以用之？公侯之宫。
被之僮僮，夙夜在公。被之祁祁，薄言还归。

草虫

喓喓草虫，趯趯阜螽。未见君子，忧心忡忡。亦既见止，亦既觏止，我心则降。
陟彼南山，言采其蕨。未见君子，忧心惙惙。亦既见止，亦既觏止，我心则说。
陟彼南山，言采其薇。未见君子，我心伤悲。亦既见止，亦既觏止，我心则夷。

采苹

于以采苹？南涧之滨。于以采藻？于彼行潦。
于以盛之？维筐及筥。于以湘之？维锜及釜。
于以奠之？宗室牖下。谁其尸之？有齐季女。

甘棠

蔽芾甘棠，勿翦勿伐，召伯所茇。
蔽芾甘棠，勿翦勿败，召伯所憩。
蔽芾甘棠，勿翦勿拜，召伯所说。

行露

厌浥行露，岂不夙夜，谓行多露。
谁谓雀无角，何以穿我屋？谁谓女无家，何以速我狱？虽速我狱，室家不足。
谁谓鼠无牙，何以穿我墉？谁谓女无家，何以速我讼？虽速我讼，亦不女从。

羔羊

羔羊之皮，素丝五紽。退食自公，委蛇委蛇。
羔羊之革，素丝五緎。委蛇委蛇，自公退食。
羔羊之缝，素丝五总。委蛇委蛇，退食自公。

殷其雷

殷其雷，在南山之阳。何斯违斯，莫敢或遑。振振君子，归哉归哉。
殷其雷，在南山之侧。何斯违斯，莫敢遑息。振振君子，归哉归哉。
殷其雷，在南山之下。何斯违斯，莫或遑处。振振君子，归哉归哉。

摽有梅

摽有梅，其实七兮。求我庶士，迨其吉兮。
摽有梅，其实三兮。求我庶士，迨其今兮。
摽有梅，顷筐墍之。求我庶士，迨其谓之。

小星

嘒彼小星，三五在东。肃肃宵征，夙夜在公。寔命不同。
嘒彼小星，维参与昴。肃肃宵征，抱衾与裯。寔命不犹。

江有汜

江有汜，之子归，不我以。不我以，其后也悔。
江有渚，之子归，不我与。不我与，其后也处。
江有沱，之子归，不我过。不我过，其啸也歌。

野有死麕

野有死麇，白茅包之。有女怀春，吉士诱之。
林有朴樕，野有死鹿，白茅纯束。有女如玉，
舒而脱脱兮，无感我帨兮，无使庬也吠。

何彼秾矣

何彼襛矣？唐棣之华。曷不肃雝？王姬之车。
何彼襛矣？华如桃李。平王之孙，齐侯之子。
其钓维何？维丝伊𦈏。齐侯之子，平王之孙。

驺虞

彼茁者葭，壹发五豝，于嗟乎驺虞。
彼茁者蓬，壹发五𫎆，于嗟乎驺虞。
en:
【Airs of the States - The Odes of Shao and the South】

The Magpie's Nest

The magpie has a nest; the turtledove dwells in it. This young lady is going to her future home; a hundred carriages are meeting her.
The magpie has a nest; the turtledove possesses it. This young lady is going to her future home; a hundred carriages are escorting her.
The magpie has a nest; the turtledove fills it. This young lady is going to her future home; a hundred carriages complete her escort.

Gathering the White Southernwood

Where go we to gather the white southernwood? In the pools and in the ponds. And what use to make of it? For the business of our princes.
Where go we to gather the white southernwood? In those valleys and in those glens. And what use to make of it? For the temples of our princes.
With head-dress reverently rising aloft, early, while yet it is night, they are in the prince's temple; in their crowded, stately array, they proceed to offer the sacrifice.

The Grasshoppers

Hear the call of the green insect, see the leap of the locusts. While I do not see my lord, my sorrowful heart is agitated. Let me but see him, let me but meet him, and my heart will then be at peace.
I ascend that hill in the south, and gather the fern-shoots there. While I do not see my lord, my sorrowful heart is very sad. Let me but see him, let me but meet him, and my heart will then be pleased.
I ascend that hill in the south, and gather the vetch-shoots there. While I do not see my lord, my sorrowful heart is wounded with grief. Let me but see him, let me but meet him, and my heart will then be at rest.

Gathering the Duckweed

Where go we to gather the duckweed? In the ditches and in the ponds. Where go we to gather the pondweed? Along the streams in the valleys.
In what are they placed? In baskets and in pans. How are they boiled? In kettles and in pans.
Where are they set? Under the window in the ancestral chamber. Who superintends the business? A reverent young lady.

The Ruler's Tree

O sweet pear-tree, do not hew it down; the chief of Shao rested under it.
O sweet pear-tree, do not break its branches; the chief of Shao rested beneath it.
O sweet pear-tree, do not bend it aside; the chief of Shao rested by it.

The Paths in the Dew

Wet and damp is the dew; - how is it that I do not wish to get away early in the night? But I fear the many paths in the dew.
Who says that the sparrow has no horn? How else could it bore through my house? Who says that you, sir, were not betrothed? How else could you have brought this suit against me? But though you have brought this suit against me, it is not sufficient for our betrothal.
Who says that the rat has no teeth? How else could it bore through my wall? Who says that you, sir, were not betrothed? How else could you have brought this action against me? But though you have brought this action against me, I will not follow you.

The Lamb's Skin

In his lamb's fur and plain silk, five braids, he goes from the court to his meals, self-satisfied and grand.
In his lamb's skin and plain silk, five braids, self-satisfied and grand, he goes from the court to his meals.
In his lamb's fur and plain silk, five braids, self-satisfied and grand, he goes from the court to his meals.

Rolling the Thunder

Rolling goes the thunder, on the south of the hill. Why is he gone away, that he is not here? My noble lord! Return, return.
Rolling goes the thunder, near the side of the hill. Why is he gone away, that he dares not take a little rest? My noble lord! Return, return.
Rolling goes the thunder, at the foot of the hill. Why is he gone away, that he dares not take a little respite? My noble lord! Return, return.

Plop Fall the Plums

Plop fall the plums; but there are still seven. Let those gentlemen that would court me come while it is lucky.
Plop fall the plums; there are still three. Let any gentleman that would court me come now.
Plop fall the plums; in shallow baskets we lay them. Any gentleman who would court me had better speak while there is time.

The Small Stars

Small are those starlets, three or five in the east. Hastily we go on our nightly march, early and late in the prince's service. Such is the difference of our lots.
Small are those starlets, Orion and the Pleiades. Hastily we go on our nightly march, carrying our coverlets and sheets. Such is the difference of our lots.

The River Has Its Branches

The river has its branches. The lady is going to be married, and will not take me with her. She will not take me with her; she will afterwards regret it.
The river has its islets. The lady is going to be married, and will not let me be with her. She will not let me be with her; she will afterwards rue it.
The river has its tributaries. The lady is going to be married, and will not let me go with her. She will not let me go with her; she will afterwards sing her sorrow.

In the Wilds Is a Dead Deer

In the wilds there is a dead deer, with white grass to wrap it. There is a young lady with thoughts natural to the spring, a fine gentleman would lead her astray.
In the forest there are the scrubby oaks; in the wilds there is a dead deer, with white grass to tie it. There is a young lady like a gem.
Slowly; gently, gently; do not move my handkerchief; do not make my dog bark.

How Great Is the Splendor

How great is the splendor! It is like the flowers of the cherry tree. How majestic is the carriage of the princess, the daughter of the king!
How great is the splendor! It is like the flowers of the peach and plum trees. She is the daughter of King Ping, the son of the marquis of Qi.
What do they use in angling? Silk threads make the lines. She is the son of the marquis of Qi, the daughter of King Ping.

The Zou Yu

How they shoot, the five boars, by the luxuriant reeds! Ah! the Zou Yu.
How they shoot, the five boars, by the luxuriant artemisia! Ah! the Zou Yu.

zh:
摘录一·中渡桥旧事
自董师处偶闻，开运三年，林文元、萧武元北上赴中渡桥，文元孤身入营劝降敌将，武元走马断桥独守单关，然滹沱战败，敌军围追堵截，二人历经艰辛，总算绝处逢生。壮志未酬，林文元一度陷入颓唐，幸有长乐老点拨，后林文元有云：经此一役方知天下为万民之天下，非士大夫之天下。
旁注一：林文元与萧武元便是在此战中崭露头角，当时文元年不过十五，文武双杰果然名不虚传。
旁注二：相传萧武元在滹沱河为保护林文元曾身负重伤，我观武元气色不佳，莫非伤势至今未愈？文津馆与青溪向来交好，当不至于袖手旁观，难道武元所中之伤无药可医？呸呸呸，乌鸦嘴……
旁注三：不知长乐老究竟是怎么开导林文元的？不知董师有没有偷听……旁听到些许内情？
……

摘录二·南北恩怨
窃听宁兄与人坐论，言及双元出身。林文元、萧武元本出身南唐世家，滹沱河一战后，二人执弟子礼拜入长乐老门下。是时正值道济先生离馆而去，长乐老对二人寄予厚望。长乐老逝后，以文津馆相托，双元为促成南北藏书合并，曾南下与诸世家交涉，然南派文人称二人作“投北叛逆”，皆避而不见。
旁注一：如今天一楼中南北藏书俱已收回，不知双元在这其中耗费多少心血？
旁注二：文人门户之见，甚于武夫械斗，惜哉！痛哉！我辈当引以为戒。
旁注三：我看那些南派文人纯纯是嫉妒，嫉妒文津馆拐走了南方最出色的少年英才！啧，这心眼子真不比针鼻儿大多少。
……
en:
Excerpt I - Faded Memories at Zhongdu Bridge

I happened to hear from Dong Shi that in the third year of Kaiyun, Laureate Lin and Champion Xiao traveled north to Zhongdu Bridge. The Laureate marched into the enemy camp alone to demand their general's surrender, while the Champion single-handedly held the broken bridge. However, the battle at Hutuo River was lost. Tracked and hunted by enemy forces, the two barely escaped with their lives. His grand ambitions thwarted, Laureate Lin fell into a deep depression, thankfully finding guidance from Elder Changle. The Laureate later remarked that the battle taught him that the realm belongs to the people, not just the noble scholars.

Note I: This battle was where Laureate Lin and Champion Xiao first made their mark. The Laureate was barely fifteen at the time. They truly live up to their reputation as the Twin Paragons of Pen and Sword.
Note II: Legend has it that Champion Xiao suffered grievous wounds at the Hutuo River while protecting Laureate Lin. The Champion still looks unwell today—perhaps his injuries never truly healed? The Inkbound Order and Silver Needle have always been on good terms, so they surely wouldn't just stand by. Is his wound truly beyond cure? Pah, I shouldn't jinx it...
Note III: I wonder how exactly Chang Lelao managed to counsel Laureate Lin? Did Dong Shi eavesdrop... or catch wind of some hidden truth?
...

Excerpt II - Feud Between North and South

I eavesdropped on Brother Ning discussing the origins of the Twin Mavens. Laureate Lin and Champion Xiao originally hailed from noble families in the Southern Tang. Following the battle at Hutuo River, they formally became disciples of Elder Changle. This happened right when Master Daoji had left the pavilion, and Elder Changle placed great hopes in both of them. Before his passing, Elder Changle entrusted the Inkbound Order to their care. Hoping to unite the literary collections of the North and South, the Twin Mavens traveled south to negotiate with the noble houses. Yet, the southern literati branded them as "Northern Traitors" and refused even to see them.

Note I: Today, the collections of both North and South are safely housed within Sky Archive. I can only imagine how much blood and sweat the Twin Mavens poured into this effort.
Note II: The sectarian prejudice among scholars is even worse than the bloody brawls of martial artists. What a tragedy! We must learn from their mistakes.
Note III: If you ask me, those southern scholars are just jealous—Jealous that the Inkbound Order snatched away their most brilliant young prodigies! Tsk, their minds are narrower than the eye of a needle.
...

Since the Tang and Song dynasties, this native apple has been a celebrated product of the Qilu region, with those grown in Qingzhou being the most exquisite. The flesh is crisp and tender, offering a sweet yet mildly tart flavor that instantly quenches thirst and clears the mind with its fresh aroma. 河岸旁能摸着野鸡蛋，能掏到搁浅的鱼。可长了书的河岸，阿芬还是第一次见。
这书沾了水，点不着了。
这书太薄，填不了肚子。
……
阿芬摇头，正要把它们一股脑全扔进河里时，芦苇中传来细碎的脚步声。
又是虏人吗？还是逃兵？阿芬一时情急，抄起一部大块头的书，随时准备要砸过去。
脚步声越来越近，一步一顿，走走停停。阿芬把书越举越高，一动也不敢动。
那人掀开了芦苇帐，显露了身形。
“莫怕，莫怕！孩子，手里那书，可否交予我看看？”
来人眼看着是个瘸子，走路尚不利索，怀里还笼了一兜书，跟阿芬手里的瞧着可像。
“这书……能卖钱？”
阿芬狐疑地盯着他。
“卖不了，”那人摇了摇头，“但得把它们留下来。留下来了，它们就是最金贵的东西。”
阿芬只听懂了“金贵”这两字。这捡书的生意，看来有做头，她阿芬也要干！
一大一小两个人影，就这样沿着河畔慢慢地走，一个捡书，一个擦书。
两人的脸都花得看不清样貌了，而那些书倒是干净得很，擦得亮亮的，就像天上的月盘一样。
en:
One could find wild eggs and stranded fish along the riverbanks. But a riverbank where books "grew" was something Fen had never seen.
These books were soaked and would not burn. They were too thin to fill a stomach.
Fen shook her head, about to throw them back into the river when faint footsteps echoed in the reeds. Was it the invaders? Or deserters? In a panic, Fen grabbed a heavy volume, ready to strike.
The footsteps drew closer, halting and slow. Fen held the book high, not daring to breathe.
The figure parted the reeds, revealing himself.
"Do not fear, child. May I look at the book in your hand?"
The stranger was a cripple who walked with a severe limp, cradling a bundle of books that looked just like Fen's.
"Can these be sold for money?" Fen asked suspiciously.
"No," the man shook his head. "But they must be preserved. If they survive, they will be the most precious treasures of all."
Fen only understood "precious." This book-salvaging business seemed promising, and she wanted in!
Two shadows, one large and one small, walked slowly along the riverbank, one gathering the books and the other wiping them clean. Their faces were smeared with mud, but the books were spotless, shining bright like the full moon.

zh:
游侠，见字如面。
前些时日，老朽随府尹大人巡查蒙学，见学堂里的娃娃们一个个正襟危坐，埋首书卷，连我等走近了都未曾察觉。
老朽心下好奇，是何等妙文，能让这些上蹿下跳的娃娃们如此专心？一问才知，他们手中所读，竟是你前些时日所赠。
老朽又问，这些书好在何处？娃娃们七嘴八舌，老朽这才知道，原来你竟为每个孩子都择了不同的书，实在是费心了。而听闻老朽与你相熟，他们都央着我，定要代他们向你道声谢。
只是，真要问他们想说什么，这群小家伙却面露羞赧，讷讷而止了。最后，老朽想了个法子，让他们把想说的话都诉诸笔端，一并封在信里了。至于写了什么，老朽绝未偷看！
对了，娃娃们还托我转交几幅画作，说是读了书卷后的有感而发。他们都说，游侠你是他们见过最有眼光的人，定能欣赏他们的大作。
哈哈，看来往后若再有与孩子们打交道的差事，找游侠准是没错了。
<IMAGE id='im1' image_url='https://h72.fp.ps.netease.com/file/68ce3ff96a0933288f80a0deKe5otW9506' size='1050*1554' color='255;255;255')'></IMAGE>

en:
Dear Wanderer,

The other day, I accompanied the Prefect on an inspection of the village school. The children sat straight at their desks, noses buried in scrolls, so absorbed they didn't even notice us draw near.
Curious what could hold their attention so completely, I asked. Turns out, they were reading the very books you gifted them not long ago.
I inquired further: what made these books so special? The little ones burst into chatter, and that's when I learned you had chosen a different book for each child. What thoughtfulness.
When they heard I knew you, they begged me to pass along their thanks.
But when I asked what they wanted to say, shyness took over, and words failed them. So I suggested they write it down instead. Their letters are enclosed. And no, I did not peek!
Oh, and they also asked me to send you a few drawings. Inspired, they said, by your books. They all agreed you're the most discerning person they've ever met, and that you'd surely appreciate their masterpieces.
Seems to me, whenever there's a task involving children, you're the one to call.

zh:
秀秀的家乡有条浅溪，阿爹从前常在夜里带她去溪边看灯尾鱼。
这种鱼天生能在浑水中寻路，鱼身一甩，尾鳍发亮，似为鱼群照明方向。
秀秀最喜欢追着这灯尾鱼看，阿爹总笑着让她跑慢些、跑慢些。
冬季水面结冰，看不成鱼，阿爹就用桃木边料雕了这尾小鱼，系上红绳挂在她颈间。
后来，契丹人来了，家成了废墟。
阿爹倒在血泊里，这一次，却喊她跑快些、跑快些。
秀秀忍住眼泪，只能继续往前跑。
如今，她跑在队伍最前头，为众人指路时，木佩总贴着心口，随步伐轻轻晃动。
她不知道自己能为多少人照亮前路，但她时常想着，只要一直往前，就当作阿爹还像从前那样，慢悠悠地笑着跟在后头吧。
en:
Xiuxiu's hometown had a shallow stream. Her father used to take her there at night to see the Lantern-tail fish.
These fish were born to find their way in murky water; with a flick of the body, their tail fins glowed, lighting the way for the school.
Xiuxiu loved chasing after them; her father always laughed and told her to slow down.
In winter, the surface froze and the fish were gone, so her father carved this little fish from peach wood scraps and hung it around her neck on a red string.
Later, The Khitans came, and home became ruins.
Father fell in a pool of blood, but this time, he shouted for her to run faster, run faster.
Xiuxiu held back her tears and could only keep running forward.
Now, as she leads the way at the front of the line, the wooden pendant hangs against her heart, swaying gently with her pace.
She doesn't know how many people she can light the way for, but she often thinks that as long as she keeps moving forward, she can pretend her father is still behind her, smiling and following slowly as he used to.

zh:
睁开眼时周遭一片漆黑，伸手不见五指——噢，伸不了手，因为此时双手正反剪在后，被沉甸甸的铁器锁住了。看来那帮恶徒对他二人还颇为敬重，不敢用麻绳，直接上了铁镣铐。陈子奚暗自发力挣扎了一下，纹丝不动，只激起一阵铁链叮当。
这动静倒是引出了身边的声音。
“这里能听到水声。我们在地下的洞里。”

“耳朵这么好，刚才怎么没听见人家放毒？”陈子奚嘴上调侃，但听到声音心里到底踏实了。
“没听到，疏忽了。”
江晏的声音离他不远，听起来没什么异样，还是一如既往波澜不惊。陈子奚失笑：“得了吧你，放毒的声音要是都能听到，你这耳朵还了得。”
他接着叹了口气：“早知道这么横冲直撞没好下场。每回跟你一块闹事就半点兵法迂回都讲不了了，由着你拔剑硬拼。要不是我脑子灵光，总能逢凶化吉……算了。你醒了多久了？”
“不久。大概半炷香。”
“半炷香，差不多该想到脱身的法子了吧？”
“没想到。”
“没想到就这么干坐着？”陈子奚深吸了一口气，望着眼前满目黑暗，开始盘算，“这帮人肯定不会光把我们丢在这儿。我们砸了那‘血判官’的场子，把他拐来的人全放跑了，他绝不肯善罢甘休，说不定待会儿就要把我俩丢去喂鳄鱼。所以说，肯定得来人。到时门一开，你就憋气装死。等他来探你鼻息，你就跳起来，把他的耳朵咬了！”

陈子奚说了半天，江晏却毫无反应。“你就说这招怎么样？”
……
“江晏？”
……
“喂，你怎么了，我看不见你——”
黑暗里幽幽传来一句：“不是你说装死吗？就像这样，对吧。”
“哈？”陈子奚愣了一下，笑出声，“还行。”

“……出去之后，”江晏忽然没头没尾接了句，“去吃城东那家爊鸭。”
“还是江大侠懂享受。”陈子奚笑得更开心了，“再切一盘橙玉生怎么样？就着丰和春下肚。”
“你哥酿的酒，闻着也不错——春蚕山庄那时候我就想尝。”
“那我去找他讨两坛。我们去西湖上喝，喝到醉了，就在水上漂着。我哥就这样。”
“不是说西湖底下有鳖精吗？”
“江大侠还怕鳖精？”
“鳖精也要斗？”
“鳖精都不斗？”

昏黑中，陈子奚的手心渐渐温热起来。他稍微活动了一下被死扣在身后的手腕。
“……反正肯定能逃出去。”陈子奚补了一句。
“逢凶化吉。”江晏的语气总像一锤定音。

山洞外忽然传来沉闷的脚步声。他和江晏对视了一眼——尽管眼前什么也看不见。
脚步声近了。
en:
Chen Zixi opened his eyes to pitch darkness. He couldn't have seen his hand in front of his face. Not that he could raise it, both arms were pinned behind his back in heavy iron shackles. Their captors clearly thought highly of the pair. Rope hadn't been enough; only iron would do. He quietly tested the bonds. Nothing moved, apart from the chains, which gave a loud rattle.
The sound drew a voice from somewhere beside him.
"I can hear water. We're in a cave underground."

"With ears like that, how did you miss them poisoning us?" Chen Zixi teased, though hearing the familiar voice was a relief.
"I didn't hear it. I wasn't careful enough."
Jiang Yan sounded close by, as calm as ever. Chen Zixi laughed. "Oh, come on. If you could actually hear someone using poison, those ears of yours would be a miracle."
He sighed. "I knew charging straight in would end badly. Every time we get into trouble together, any hope of tactics goes out the window. Out comes your sword, and in we go. If I weren't so quick on my feet, always finding us a way out... Never mind. How long have you been awake?"
"Not long. About half a stick of incense."
"Half a stick? Long enough to come up with an escape plan, surely?"
"I haven't."
"So you've just been sitting here?" Chen Zixi took a deep breath and stared into the darkness, thinking. "They won't leave us here forever. We wrecked the Blood Judge's operation and freed everyone he'd abducted. He won't let that go. He might even feed us to the crocodiles. Anyway, someone will come. When the door opens, hold your breath and play dead. As soon as he leans in to check your breathing, jump up and bite his ear!"

After all that, Jiang Yan still hadn't said a word. "Well? What do you think?"
...
"Jiang Yan?"
...
"Hey, what's wrong? I can't see you..."
A quiet voice came out of the darkness. "You told me to play dead. Like that, right?"
"Huh?" Chen Zixi paused, then burst out laughing. "Not bad."

"...When we get out," Jiang Yan said suddenly, "let's get braised duck. That place on the east side of the city."
"Now there's a man who knows how to enjoy himself." Chen Zixi's grin widened. "How about a plate of Citrine Delight as well? With some Spring's Bounty to wash it down."
"Your brother's wine smells good too. I've wanted to try it ever since Silkworm Manor."
"Then I'll ask him for a couple of jars. We'll take a boat onto West Lake and drink ourselves silly. Then we can just drift. That's what my brother does."
"Isn't there a turtle spirit at the bottom of West Lake?"
"What, the great Jiang Yan is afraid of a turtle spirit?"
"You'd pick a fight with a turtle spirit too?"
"You'd let a turtle spirit stop you?"

In the darkness, warmth began to spread through Chen Zixi's palms. He shifted his wrists a little inside the shackles behind his back.
"...We'll get out. We always do," he added.
"Always a way out." As ever, Jiang Yan spoke as though that settled it.

Heavy footsteps sounded outside the cave. He and Jiang Yan looked at each other, though neither could see a thing.
The footsteps drew closer.
Liang Pai Zhuai

zh:
冯道顿首再拜鹤先生足下：

春山寂寂，松涛如诉。自君骑鹤归去，忽已三稔。每忆昔年共论稷下遗风，君以“教化天下”为志，今封龙山庄诸生星散四方，颇得薪传之效，谨为君陈之。

淮阳杨生悫，得君亲授，今立学社于陈州。聚徒讲习，重建庠序之制，乡绅负笈而至者甚众，俨然有齐鲁遗风。

庐山李善道，携君所赠书卷南游，结庐五老峰下，白鹿洞中弦诵不绝，江州士子多裹粮从之。其余如岳麓、嵩阳诸地，皆有草堂新起，缥缃映野，诵声晨昏相应。

道尝观天象，见文曲芒动于中原。昔者君言“门闼之锢非斧钺可破”，今则隙光已透，清风徐入。虽无锋镝之变，而向学之风渐盛，此诚君廿载心血所凝。

然山河依旧，独少青鹤唳空。每见封龙山下新竹破石，辄思君植杖观耘之态。门生列籍如云，竟无人得见君临阶抚卷——此道心中长憾也。

时雨既降，而播雨者未知润物之功；星火已燃，然举火者不见燎原之势。悲夫！惟以樽酒酹君当年执炬处。

临楮怅然，不知所云。
en:
With deepest reverence, Feng Dao bows before Master Crane:

The spring mountains lie in silence, and the winds through the pines sound like weeping. It has been three years since you rode the crane into the distance. I often recall our old discussions on the ancient scholastic ideals, where you vowed to "enlighten all under heaven." Today, the disciples of Dragonbend Academy have scattered across the realm, successfully passing on the torch of your teachings. I write to respectfully report this to you.

Yang Que of Huaiyang, who received your direct instruction, has now established a scholarly society in Chenzhou. He gathers pupils and has restored the local academies; countless gentry travel miles with books on their backs to attend, vividly recreating the revered scholastic spirit of old.

Li Shandao of Lushan journeyed south bearing the scrolls you bestowed upon him. He built a retreat beneath the Five Elders Peak, and the sound of chanting echoes endlessly from the White Deer Cave. Scholars from Jiangzhou pack their own rations just to follow him. In other lands like Yuelu and Songyang, new thatched academies are constantly rising. Books gleam across the fields, and the sounds of recitation answer each other from dawn to dusk.

I have observed the heavens and seen the Literary Star shining brightly over the Central Plains. You once said, "The shackles upon the mind's gate cannot be shattered by axes and halberds." Now, a sliver of light has pierced through, and a clear breeze blows gently in. Though there has been no clash of arms, the thirst for knowledge flourishes. This is truly the culmination of your twenty years of blood and sweat.

Yet the rivers and mountains remain the same, lacking only the cry of the azure crane in the sky. Whenever I see new bamboo breaking through the rocks at the foot of Dragonbend Mountain, I picture you leaning on your staff, quietly watching the fields. Disciples now gather like clouds, but none have the fortune to see you step up to the hall with a book in hand. This will forever be the greatest regret in my heart.

The timely rain has fallen, but the one who seeded the clouds knows not the grace it brings; the spark has been struck, but the one who lit it cannot see the prairie ablaze. How deeply it grieves me! I can only pour this cup of wine upon the earth, right where you once held the torch.

As my brush touches the paper, my heart is lost in sorrow, and I know not what else to say.

zh:
游侠亲启：

今儿个天还没亮透，我还就被福禄寿三个小家伙给闹醒啦！她们说要赶个早，给大个子写信。
没睡醒归没睡醒，但这大过年的，热闹点好啊！
先给游侠拜个年——祝新春大吉，万事胜意，福气满堂！
好了，接下来是孩子们要对你说的话。老朽不敢怠慢，这就逐字记下：
小福： 嘿嘿！集主好厉害哇！咱们百味集办得……怎么说来着？呃，对了！办得红红火火，喜气洋洋！
小寿： 别憋词儿了！轮到下一个啦，小禄说！
小禄： 嗯……小禄想说……今年过年最难忘的，是结识了新朋友呢。以后阿宗、阿然都是咱们的好玩伴啦。
阿然悄悄告诉我，虽然看不见，但她能听出来，烟花是五颜六色的，暖烘烘的，一直亮到了梦里头。
小寿： 到我啦！大个子，昨晚我们三姐妹做了同一个梦。我们飞到了天上，比烟花还要高！低头一瞧，满城的人都在笑，你也在笑，笑得可开心啦！我们把梦里看到的好风景都画下来啦，送给你！
<IMAGE id='im1' image_url='https://h72.fp.ps.netease.com/file/697b3f7bc9127f5f2de4b9b8cGfZeh7J07' size='1920*1080' color='255;255;255')'></IMAGE>
这幅画我看明白了！这是鱼龙曼延，春暖人间呐！
这场百味集，孩子们喜欢得很，我看着也心里热乎。希望这百味暖春常伴游侠，年年欢喜！
en:
Dear Wanderer,

The day had yet to fully dawn when I was roused by those three little kids, Fu, Lu, and Shou!
Fatigued as I may be, it is the New Year after all. The more bustle and joy, the better!
Allow me to offer my greetings first. May the New Year bring you grand fortune, may all your wishes be fulfilled, and may blessings fill your halls!
Okay, now for what the kids want to say. I'm writing it down exactly the way they said it:
Little Fu: The Feast Master is so incredible! Our Flavor Feast was... how do you say it? Ah, right! It was flourishing and brimming with festive joy!
Little Shou: Stop struggling for words! It's the next one's turn. Little Lu, go!
Little Lu: Hmm... What I want to say is... the best thing about this New Year was making new friends. From now on, A'zong and Ran are our playmates. Ran whispered to me that although she cannot see, she can hear that the fireworks are colorful and warm, glowing all the way into her dreams.
Little Shou: Now's my turn! Big friend, we had the same dream last night. In our dream, we flew up into the heavens, higher even than the fireworks! We saw the entire city down there was filled with smiles, and you were laughing so happily, too! We drew all the beautiful things we saw in the dream for you!
<IMAGE id='im1' image_url='https://h72.fp.ps.netease.com/file/697b3f7bc9127f5f2de4b9b8cGfZeh7J07' size='1920*1080' color='255;255;255')'></IMAGE>
Now, this painting I understand! It is the Beast Reverie, the warmth of spring returning to the world!
The children truly enjoy the Flavor Feast, and their joy warmed my heart. May this warm spring of flavors always be there for you, bringing you happiness year after year!
Contracted the illness after a disruption in moisture balance.

zh:
从一座空墓中掘出的短刃，柄上缠着褪色的红绳。
墓主的武功秘籍堆叠如小山，每一册扉页上都用狂躁的字迹反复写着同一个女人的名字——以及“烦死了”“可恨”之类的随笔。
那个叫狐令飞的墓主，生前自认傲视江湖，却唯独在这几行字里露出了败相。
阿狄学了几本武功，又割下其中一页，将它塞进怀中最贴身的位置。
撞见了如此奇遇的他毅然攥着匕首走出荒山。
他想，既然那个女人曾令狐令飞如此不甘，那么被关在岱山的她——或许缺一个徒弟。
一个像他这样的徒弟。
en:
A short blade dug up from an empty tomb, with a faded red cord wrapped around its hilt.
The tomb owner's martial arts manuals were stacked like a little mountain. On the title page of every single one, the name of the same woman was furiously scribbled over and over—along with random notes like "so annoying" and "how hateful."
That tomb owner, Hu Lingfei, believed himself unparalleled in the martial world while alive, yet he showed his defeat solely within these few lines.
Adi learned a few of the martial arts, tore out one of the pages, and tucked it away right next to his chest.
After stumbling upon something so incredible, he gripped the dagger tightly and marched out of those barren mountains.
He figured, if that woman could make Hu Lingfei so bitter, then she—the one locked up in Mount Tai—might just need a disciple.
A disciple just like him.

en:
To my daughter Yiming, a blessing upon your coming of age.

If I have not yet returned, then this campaign I ride with the General is likely lost. I was born of this land and shall die for it. I have no regrets. The red tassel given to me by the General—I have left a strand of it for you in this box. Should you ever face hardship, take this to him. He will surely help you.

Before my departure, I instructed Rena to bring you to this well on your birthday, to make a wish and receive the gift I left. When you received them... I hope they brought you joy.

And Rena... your Ana, is she well? If the desert winds have scattered my letters home, then speak these words for her: She is the most beautiful and courageous woman in all the desert. And when I become the wind and sand, I will carry all my lost longings and strive with all my might to return to her side.

If you read this, and I am beside you, we shall watch the stars together tonight. If I am not, then please, wear this hairpin, and let the stars be my eyes to look upon you.

It will suit you perfectly.

zh:
契丹铁骑踏入清河时，仇越海应了烈言之请，一同抗击外敌。
是夜，百草野外，烈言点燃篝火，以天地为席，与仇越海相对而饮。
他们都曾是漂泊江湖的浪荡子，而今为了一件事，萍聚一处，倒像是一见如故的老友。
酒酣耳热，仇越海纵身挑枪，横抹而出，要与烈言决个高下。烈言因着酒力正涌，身形微晃，醉步难持。却见他探手抽刀，刀势连绵，如能断水。横截来路，斜斩去势。身影交错间，寒月亦为之晦明。
二人此来彼往，酣畅淋漓，一时难分胜负。连不善言辞的古乐都看得怔住，待二人收势，方叹问道，烈言兄这刀法，师承何处？
“无门无派，不过是旧日独饮，醉里偶得罢了。今日与仇兄一较，倒让我这刀法进益不少。”烈言洒然一笑，将坛中余酒一饮而尽。
野风骤起，吹散酒气，百草伏而复立。此间旧事，风过无迹，唯明月曾流照。
en:
When the Khitan cavalry swept into Qinghe, Qiu Yuehai answered Lie Yan's call, joining blades to hold back the foreign tide.
That night, deep in the Verdant Wilds, Lie Yan built a campfire. With the earth as their seat and the vast night sky as their canopy, the two men sat across from one another and drank.
Both were once vagabonds, adrift in the jianghu. Yet, drawn together by a single cause, they found an instant kinship, like old friends reunited.
Flushed with wine, Qiu Yuehai leapt to his feet. With a sweeping flourish of his spear, he challenged Lie Yan to a test of skill. Heavy with drink, Lie Yan swayed, his drunken steps faltering. Yet in a flash, he drew his saber. The momentum of his blade was a ceaseless, unbroken dance, so fluid it seemed it could sever a flowing stream. He swept horizontally to parry the incoming thrusts, and slashed diagonally to break his opponent's charge. As their clashing silhouettes blurred together, even the cold moonlight seemed to flicker in their wake.
They traded blows to their hearts' content, perfectly matched and locked in a glorious stalemate. Even the taciturn Gu Le was spellbound. Only when the men finally lowered their weapons did he exhale in awe, asking, "Brother Lie Yan, from what master did you learn such a blade technique?"
"No master, no sect," Lie Yan said. "It is merely something I stumbled upon in my lonely cups. Though, crossing blades with Brother Qiu tonight has certainly sharpened its edge." With a carefree smile, he tipped his jar and drained the last of the wine.
A sudden gale swept across the plains, scattering the scent of wine as the wild grass bowed and rose again. Like the wind, the deeds of that night passed without a trace, leaving nothing behind save for the bright moon that once shone down upon them.

昔吾游历八荒，见奇草异木，或有可致长生者。乃夜谒董公，
自请重游，若能得仙桃一枚，仙酒半卮，延帝寿百年，或可稍宽上心，重为明主矣。

en:
Sixth month, second year of Yuanfeng.
In my youth, I served His Majesty and watched him subdue the border tribes and expand our frontiers, knowing he was no ordinary sovereign. Yet as His Majesty grew old, dread of death took hold. He placed his faith in alchemists and sought immortals, exhausting the people and squandering the treasury, heedless of all counsel. The scholars of the Confucian court were consumed with despair, yet seeking guidance from Lord Dong brought no remedy.
Having roamed the far wilderness in my earlier days, I had seen strange herbs and wondrous flora, some perhaps holding the secret to long life. Thus, I visited Lord Dong by night, volunteering to travel once more. If I could procure a single immortal peach or half a cup of immortal wine to extend His Majesty's life by a century, it might ease his mind and restore him as a wise ruler.
Lord Dong was displeased, but ultimately consented.

It should have been a place of peace, but blood has reached its soil.

观里的小道士分它一口饭吃，它作为回报，会帮他们抓偷吃香烛的小老鼠。
本来猫和人相安无事，日子挺好的。但那个小道士来了以后，一切都变了。
他说它像天边的一道云，总也抓不住，非要给它取名叫白云。
白云起初并不乐意。但那小道士叽叽喳喳的，好生吵闹。为了得份清净，它只好勉强接受了。

White Cloud had no name at first. 
She liked the scent of sandalwood, the sound of temple bells, and so followed the city wall until she reached Palace of Supreme Oneness. 
There, a young priest shared his meal with her. In return, she caught the mice that tried to nibble on candles. 
Life was peaceful. Cat and human in harmony. Until that young Daoist arrived and ruined everything. 
He said she was unreachable like a drifting cloud in the sky. He insisted on naming her "White Cloud." 
At first, she didn't like it. But the Daoist was noisy, always chattering. So for some peace and quiet, she reluctantly accepted it.

zh:
本想借此番云游，让鸽白尼好好修习一番和善待人的功夫。哪料竟从盖琮和喻孑处听闻，它日日卯时起身，勤勉得很——结果反被放了鸽子，从此一蹶不振。
唉！可见有些事即便两厢情愿，也难免横生变故，乃至阴差阳错，一误再误。非是那鸽子有意要鸽，实在是那一纸一信上写的多是些无奈之辞。泣之，怜之。
此事怪我思虑不周，倒叫这孩子受了委屈……还请游侠得空时宽慰它几句。鸽白尼向来好哄，我教游侠一招：若见它又郁郁早起，便灌它一壶“卯时酒”，保管让它昏昏醉到酉，一鸽便是一整日，什么烦心事也都忘了。
墨点无多泪点多，鸽子仍是旧鸽子。想来经此一事，游侠也能理解一二了。与游侠所约，百忙之余仍是百忙，咱们便下回再叙！一定！
en:
I'd hoped this trip would help Dovernicus learn a thing or two about kindness and getting along with others. Instead, I heard from Gai Cong and Yu Jie that it had been waking at dawn every single day, diligent as could be, only to end up being stood up, and taking the blow so hard it still hasn't quite recovered.
Some things go wrong no matter how much both sides may want them to work out. A little bad timing here, a little bad luck there, and before you know it, one misunderstanding turns into another. It wasn't that the other pigeon meant to leave it hanging; those letters were full of helpless apologies more than anything else. All one can do is feel sorry for the poor thing.
This was my fault for not thinking things through. The child ended up hurt because of me... If you have a spare moment, Ranger, do try to cheer it up a little. Dovernicus has always been easy enough to comfort, and I'll let you in on a trick: if you see it getting up early again looking gloomy, give it a flask of "dawn wine." I guarantee it'll stay pleasantly muddled all the way till dusk, flaking the whole day away in a haze, with every worry forgotten.
There may not be much ink on the page, but there are plenty of tears. That pigeon is still the same old pigeon, after all. I imagine this whole affair has helped you understand a thing or two as well. As for the time I promised you, well, even in the middle of all my busyness, I remain terribly busy. So let's catch up next time! Definitely!

醉拳客原名陈全，是鬼街十四煞中，最肆意潇洒的一个。

他在地里打滚的那几年，正逢乱世，又遭饥荒，日子实在称不上好。但他随他父母，最会苦中作乐。于醉拳客而言，世间万物，皆有个中乐趣。而其中最者，唯酒是也。醉时见天见地，如梦似幻，更添趣味。但他这般心性，不免遭人诟病。有人在他醉时来寻麻烦。这可好，反叫他在醉中领悟出了一套别样的功法。

有些游手好闲之士听了此事，大感好奇，常来寻他比划。长此以往，他便渐渐打响了醉拳客的名号。但醉拳客对什么名号啊，江湖啊，都不甚在意。只要日日有酒，再交几个好友，那便是，最最畅快的一生了。
en:
The Drunk Martial Artist, known as Chen Quan, was the most carefree and unrestrained among the Fourteen Fiends of Ghost Street.

During his early years rolling through the dirt fields, the world was gripped by war and famine. Life was far from easy. Yet Chen Quan and his parents knew well how to find joy in hardship. To the Drunk Martial Artist, there was delight hidden in all things. But of all delights, none compared to wine. When drunk, he could see heaven and earth, dreams and reality blending into a wild, wondrous mix. Of course, such a nature deserved its share of criticism. Some sought him out when he was drunk, looking for trouble. Yet that only encouraged him to eventually invent a style of his own, a martial art born from the haze of wine.

Word spread among wanderers, and many came seeking to spar with him, eager to test his unique skills. Over time, the title Drunk Martial Artist grew louder across the jianghu. But Chen Quan himself couldn't care less for titles or the jianghu. So long as he had wine by his side, and a few good friends to share it with, that was all he needed. The most joyful life he could ever ask for.

我乃孤云弟子，今不幸困死此处，留书以助后人。
第一日，沙场点兵，战的痛快。以为战完，即可出关。
谁知战至十数回，胜负皆有，战后，又重回军鼓处。
如此循环往复。
后坐守粮草塔一日，观守军搬粮十五次。离开即止。
坐城楼一日，箭矢一刻未停。离开即止。
自第一日算起，已循环四十九次，所试逃脱之法不知凡几，无果。
城中枯骨不止百余，恐怕皆是被诓至此的武林同道。
或有留书，或有石刻，多毁于风沙。
探查至今，毫无头绪。只知关键所在安西军处，在郭昕处……
en:
I am a disciple of Lone Cloud, trapped here and fated to die. May this writing serve those who follow me into this place.

On the first day, we mustered on the field and fought with valor. I presumed that once the battle was won, we could leave the pass.
But after scores of battles, through both victory and defeat, we found ourselves returned to the place where the war drums sound. It is a loop without end.

I have kept watch. For one day, I stood guard at the supply tower and saw the soldiers move grain fifteen times. The moment I stepped away, they stopped. For another, I sat atop the city tower as arrows rained down without pause. The moment I left, they ceased.
It has been forty-nine days, forty-nine cycles. My attempts to escape have been countless, and all have failed.

This city is a graveyard for hundreds. They were likely martial artists like myself, drawn into this trap. Some left notes, others carvings, but the wind and sand have claimed most of them.

To this day, I have found no answers. I know only this: the secret lies with the Anxi Army, and with Guo Xin.

zh: “天下之无道也久矣，天将以夫子为木铎。”唐天祐二年，朱温窃窥十相之书，谋而未遂，遂酿白马之祸。文津馆预得其情，乃命诸弟子各携典籍，四散乡野，藏于民间。厥后数十载，历三代文元备尝艰辛，始次第寻回诸书。 长乐老于天一楼侧建木铎钟楼。间有时日，令弟子击钟，钟声既作，凡在门之徒，无论身寄何处、所司何事，皆须星驰至楼前，领一册书，携往安处。此名曰“先贤仪”。仪之设也，既以志其事，亦以演习其事，使后来者永怀“木铎”传道之责，毋或忘焉。
en: "Long has the Way been absent from the world. Heaven shall make the Master its Clarion Chime." In the second year of Tianyu, Zhu Wen cast covetous eyes upon the Ten Sages' Collection, plotting to seize it, yet his scheme came to naught, and in its wake the Baima Incident was wrought. The Inkbound Order, having learned of his designs in advance, ordered its disciples to each take up volumes of the sacred texts and scatter to the countryside, hiding them among the common folk. In the decades that followed, three generations of Laureate endured untold hardship before the texts were recovered, one by one. Elder Changle raised a bell tower beside Tianyi Tower. At intervals of his choosing, he would bid a disciple strike the bell, and when its sound rang out, all those within the Order, wherever they dwelt or whatever their duties, were to hasten with all speed to the tower, receive one volume, and carry it to a place of safety. This rite was named the "Rite of the Sages." The ceremony was established both to commemorate what had come to pass and to rehearse it anew, so that those who came after would forever hold in their hearts the duty of the Clarion Chime, to carry the Way forward, and never let it be forgotten.

en:
To the kind soul who finds this letter,

Greetings.
My name is Zhan Yuelu. Lately, it has not been easy for me to get around, and my messenger dove often loses its way, so I hope you might do me a favor. I've enclosed a small packet of pine nuts and acorns as thanks, and I hope you'll kindly accept it.

There's one more letter as well. Please help deliver it to Tuo, who lives on the hillside outside Mohist City. The weather is turning cold, and Tuo has not come to Stellabed Rocks for quite some time. Grandma may only remember him now and then, but she truly misses him deep down. Thank you for making the trip on my behalf. If you have the time, do come by Stellabed Rocks sometime, and I'll treat you to a meal.

Oh, and could I trouble you to ask Tuo one more thing? Last time, he promised to tell me the story of the "Nameless Wanderer." When will he finally tell it to me?

《悬剑空垄》

季札心知之，为使上国，未献。
还至徐，徐君已死，于是乃解其宝剑，系之徐君冢树而去。
从者曰：“徐君已死，尚谁予乎？”
季子曰：“不然。始吾心已许之，岂以死倍吾心哉！”
en:
When Ji Zha first set out on his mission, he passed north through the state of Xu. The Lord of Xu coveted Ji Zha's sword, but dared not speak his desire.
Ji Zha knew this in his heart, yet as he was on a mission to vassal states, he did not offer the sword.
Upon his return to Xu, the Lord of Xu had died. So Ji Zha unbuckled his sword and tied it to a tree by the lord's tomb before departing.
His attendant asked: "The Lord of Xu is dead. Who will you give this to now?"
Ji Zha replied: "Not so. My heart had already promised it to him. How could I betray my heart because he died?"

zh:

那是权臣给这位江湖侠客的见面礼。

惊涛掌未曾收过这么重的礼，左思右想，最后把这珠子缀在了给女儿的新鞋上。
但兰澳扯掉了明珠，将那华贵的珠宝丢了出去，珠子咕噜噜滚过客栈油腻腻的过道，依然不改它的明光。
无论是糊里糊涂收下礼物的父亲，还是不明所以但是就是不喜欢的女儿，
那时候他们都不知道，上位者所有的馈赠，都会让你付出昂贵的代价。或早或晚。
en:
The brocade recalls what they were made to be, and the wear tells the story of all the years they've traveled through. 
When the father gifted these shoes, he attached two glowing pearls to the toes— 
gifts from a powerful noble to a wanderer. 

Palm Strike Master had never received such a lavish present before. After much thought, he fastened the pearls to a new pair intended for his daughter. 
But Lan Ao tore them away, tossing the precious jewels to the dusty floor, where they rolled across the greasy inn hallway, still shining with unyielding light. 
Neither the bewildered father who accepted the gift, nor the daughter who rejected it, 
understood then that such favors from the mighty always came with a hidden price—one paid sooner or later.

zh:
今日突发！东方第一枝接得一封来信，信中所述，无不令人称奇……
寄信人自称任长安，言其昨夜于梦中行至大漠，忽见一将军，金纹披甲，须眉如雪。将军竟知冰食，道此物自古有之，乃边关将领防暑之法。
将军托梦传方，然长安一梦，醒之皆忘，唯记此句：“若于日中饮之，则凉意贯身，暑气不侵！”
此事真假，尚不可考。然余手中尚存冰食二两，遂依信中之法亲试其效——果真凉气拂身，暑意全消！
至此，东方第一枝发布天下召告：恳请神秘男子来东风楼一叙，愿共研冰食，以济苍生！
en:
Urgent Report! Eastern First Branch received a letter today, its contents nothing short of extraordinary...
The sender, one Ren Chang'an, claims to have wandered a desert in his dreams last night, where he encountered a snow-bearded general clad in gilded armor. The general spoke of Frostbite, an ancient remedy used by frontier commanders to ward off heatstroke.
Though the dream faded upon waking, one phrase lingered: "Drink it under the noon sun, and chill shall pierce your veins, repelling all summer's fury!"
Its truth remains unverified. Yet, with two taels of Frostbite still in hand, I tested the method described—indeed, a wave of coolness swept over me, banishing the heat entirely!
Thus, Eastern First Branch proclaims to the realm: We summon the Mysterious Man to East Wind Pavilion to collaborate on Frostbite, for the salvation of all!

墨守亭中说春秋，辩经台前论古今。近来山中风雨飘摇，开山与封山之辩，亦成为弟子平日讨论的焦点。
你本已习惯这般情境，路过此亭时，却见到熟悉的身影被团团围住——左边为首之人高呼封山，右边领头的则大喊开山，冯大哥正夹在其中左右为难。
你知道他一向不喜争辩，便走上前去替他解围：
#Y【封山好！】若心系天下众生，则墨门弟子亦是天下众生之一，不先护好自家人，如何护天下人？#E
众人听罢皆为之一怔，趁他们尚在回味中，你一口气把冯大哥拉出了人群。气息平复后，你左看右看，总觉得冯大哥有了些变化，却说不上来。适逢一阵强风吹来，冯大哥摸了摸自己的脑袋——
好消息是，冯大哥虽潜心科研，但头发依旧很茂密！
坏消息是，冯大哥的帽子被落在亭子里了……
en:
At Confluence Gazebo, they recount history; at the Disputation Platform, they debate the ages. With storms brewing of late, the debate between Expansion and Seclusion has become the center of daily discourse.
Accustomed to such scenes, you are passing the place when you spot a familiar figure surrounded by a clamoring crowd. To the left, voices clamor to seal the gate; to the right, they shout to open it. Caught in the middle, Feng is in a total bind.
Knowing his distaste for disputes, you step forward to bail him out:
#Y[Seclusion!] If we care for all living souls, are we not souls ourselves? If we cannot protect our own kin, how can we protect the world?#E
The crowd falls into a stunned silence. Seizing the moment while they reflect, you pull Feng through the throng in one swift motion. Once your breath is caught, you look him up and down. Something about Feng seems different, though you can't quite put your finger on it. Just then, a gust of wind sweeps by. Feng instinctively feels his head...
The good news: despite his devotion to research, Feng's hair remains thick and lush!
The bad news: his hat was left behind in Confluence Gazebo...

zh:
开运二年秋，江、陈二人难得偷闲，寻了处深山竹林，相约一道喝酒。乡野小村中农家自酿的高粱酒，入口烈而味酸涩。江晏喝了几口顿觉无趣，只叹如今天下动荡，那些品酒、酿酒之人皆无心入世，竟连一杯好酒都难求。陈子奚可不似江晏这般，纵使这酒粗劣，他还是用小盏细细品着。

“此情此景，与尔共饮，岂非美酒乎？若是得了好酒却发现身边无人，不更可惜？”

见江晏并未作答，陈子奚兀自举盏笑道：“也罢，总归还有我同你一道。”
en:
During the autumn of the second year of Kaiyun, Jiang Yan and Chen Zixi managed to steal a rare moment of leisure. Deep in a mountain bamboo grove, the two shared a quiet drink. The sorghum wine, brewed by villagers nearby, was harsh on the tongue and tinged with sourness. Jiang took a few sips before setting his cup down in disappointment. He lamented how the world's turmoil had robbed winemakers of heart and purpose, leaving even a good drink hard to come by. But Chen Zixi was not like Jiang Yan. Even with such crude wine, he sipped slowly from his small cup, savoring it with care. 

"This wine, this moment, and a friend beside me. Isn't that enough to make it fine? What good is the finest drink, if there's no one to share it with?" 

Seeing that Jiang Yan did not answer, Chen Zixi raised his cup and laughed.
"Well then, at least you still have me."

zh: 悬泉驿雄峙玉门关外，汉时称悬泉置，唐复称悬泉驿。处安西入西域道，掌音书并军政车马。其址有山谷，内有悬泉如练，飞漱苍岩，故而得名悬泉驿。贞观间，唐军重葺驿垣，立箭楼、筑马厩，自此霜矛映日，铁骑驰烟。每逢朔风卷碛之时，驿卒执虎符疾驰，驼铃刀剑相杂。后西戎犯境，音书断绝，悬泉驿枯守瀚海，终毁于战火。箭痕深镌石壁，血沁犹染驿砖。今临残垣，唯见孤泉涸迹，荒草萋萋。残垣断瓦，满目尘烟，沉舟如林，不复人烟。
en:
Celestial Spring Station stands towering outside Jade Gate Pass. Known as Celestial Spring Post in the Han Dynasty, it was renamed Celestial Spring Station during the Tang. Located on the route from Anxi to the Western Regions, it handled correspondence, military affairs, and transport.

The station sits in a valley where a spring cascades down verdant cliffs like silk, thus earning its name "Celestial Spring."

During the Zhenguan reign, the Tang army rebuilt the station walls, erected watchtowers, and constructed stables. Frost-tipped spears gleamed in sunlight; iron cavalry thundered through dust and smoke. When northern winds swept the desert, couriers raced with tiger tallies, the jingle of camel bells mingling with the clink of swords and sabers.

Later, tribes from the Western Regions invaded, severing all communication. Celestial Spring Station stood guard over the barren expanse until war consumed it. Arrow scars remain etched in stone; bloodstains still mark the bricks.

Today, approaching the ruins, one only sees the dried traces of the lonely spring and overgrown weeds. Broken walls and tiles, dust and smoke everywhere, abandoned carts lie like a forest, and no human trace remains.

Its students must read deeply of the past, drawing lessons from history to illuminate the present, and must sharpen a keen eye for the people, affairs, and things of today. Its students must commit the statutes and precedents of every dynasty to memory, and hold fast to the principle of virtuous conduct and measured punishment. The three great Study Halls have developed countless talents for the world.

zh:
【桓公第二】

【经】
元年，春，王正月，公即位。
○三月，公会郑伯于垂。郑伯以璧假许田。
○夏，四月，丁未，公及郑伯盟于越。
○秋，大水。
○冬，十月。
【传】
元年，春，公即位，修好于郑。郑人请复祀周公，卒易祊田。公许之。三月，郑伯以璧假许田，为周公、祊故也。
○夏，四月，丁未，公及郑伯盟于越，结祊成也。盟曰：“渝盟，无享国！”
○秋，大水。凡平原出水为大水。
○冬，郑伯拜盟。
○宋华父督见孔父之妻于路，目逆而送之，曰：“美而艳。”

【经】
二年，春，王正月，戊申，宋督弑其君与夷及其大夫孔父。
○滕子来朝。
○三月，公会齐侯、陈侯、郑伯于稷，以成宋乱。
○夏，四月，取郜大鼎于宋。戊申，纳于大庙。
○秋，七月，杞侯来朝。
○蔡侯、郑伯会于邓。
○九月，入耜。
○公及戎盟于唐。冬，公至自唐。
【传】
二年，春，宋督攻孔氏，杀孔父而取其妻。公怒，督惧，遂弑殇公。君子以督为有无君之心，而后动于恶，故先书弑其君。会于稷，以成宋乱。为赂故，立华氏也。
宋殇公立，十年十一战，民不堪命。孔父嘉为司马，督为太宰，故因民之不堪命，先宣言曰：“司马则然。”已杀孔父而弑殇公，召庄公于郑而立之，以亲郑。以郜大鼎赂公，齐、陈、郑皆有赂，故遂相宋公。
夏，四月，取郜大鼎于宋。戊申，纳于大庙，非礼也。臧哀伯谏曰：“君人者将昭德塞违，以临照百官，犹惧或失之，故昭令德以示子孙。是以清庙茅屋，大路越席，大羹不致，粢食不凿，昭其俭也。衮、冕、黻、珽，带、裳、幅、舄，衡、𬘘、纮、𫄧，昭其度也。藻率、鞞、琫，鞶、厉、游、缨，昭其数也。火、龙、黼、黻，昭其文也。五色比象，昭其物也。钖、鸾、和、铃，昭其声也。三辰旗旗，昭其明也。夫德，俭而有度，登降有数，文物以纪之，声明以发之，以临照百官。百官于是乎戒惧，而不敢易纪律。今灭德立违，而置其赂器于大庙，以明示百官，百官象之，其又何诛焉？国家之败，由官邪也；官之失德，宠赂章也。郜鼎在庙，章孰甚焉？武王克商，迁九鼎于雒邑，义士犹或非之，而况将眧违乱之赂器于大庙，其若之何？”公不听。
周内史闻之，曰：“臧孙达其有后于鲁乎！君违，不忘谏之以德。”
○秋，七月，耜侯来朝，不敬。耜侯归，乃谋伐之。
○蔡侯、郑伯会于邓，始惧楚也。
○九月，入耜，讨不敬也。
○公及戎盟于唐，修旧好也。冬，公至自唐，告于庙也。凡公行，告于宗庙，反行，饮至、舍爵、策勋焉，礼也。特相会，往来称地，让事也。自参以上，则往称地，来称会，成事也。
○初，晋穆侯之夫人姜氏以条之役生大子，命之曰仇。其弟以千亩之战生，命之曰成师。师服曰：“异哉，君之名子也。夫名以制义，义以出礼，礼以体政，政以正民。是以政成而民听，易则生乱。嘉耦曰妃，怨耦曰仇，古之命也。今君命大子曰仇，弟曰成师，始兆乱矣。兄其替乎？”
惠之二十四年，晋始乱，故封桓叔于曲沃，靖侯之孙栾宾傅之。师服曰：“吾闻国家之立也，本大而末小，是以能固。故天子建国，诸侯立家，卿置侧室，大夫有贰宗，士有隶子弟，庶人、工、商各有分亲，皆有等衰。是以民服事其上，而下无觊觎。今晋，甸侯也，而建国，本既弱矣，其能久乎？”
惠之三十年，晋潘父弑昭侯而纳桓叔，不克。晋人立孝侯。惠之四十五年，曲沃庄伯伐翼，弑孝侯。翼人立其弟鄂侯。鄂侯生哀侯。哀侯侵陉庭之田。陉庭南鄙启曲沃伐翼。

en:
【Duke Huan, Year 2】

【Classic】
First year, spring, the king's first month, the Duke assumed the throne.
○ In the third month, the Duke met with the Earl of Zheng at Chui. The Earl of Zheng used a jade disc to exchange for the fields of Xu.
○ Summer, fourth month, Dingwei day, the Duke and the Earl of Zheng swore an alliance at Yue.
○ Autumn, great flood.
○ Winter, tenth month.
【Commentary】
First year, spring, the Duke assumed the throne and restored good relations with Zheng. The people of Zheng requested to resume the sacrifices to the Duke of Zhou and finally exchange the fields of Beng. The Duke agreed. In the third month, the Earl of Zheng used a jade disc to exchange for the fields of Xu, for the sake of the Duke of Zhou and Beng.
○ Summer, fourth month, Dingwei day, the Duke and the Earl of Zheng swore an alliance at Yue, to conclude the agreement over Beng. The oath said: "If one breaks this alliance, may he not enjoy his state!"
○ Autumn, great flood. Generally, when water overflows the plains, it is called a great flood.
○ Winter, the Earl of Zheng came to thank the Duke for the alliance.
○ Hua Fudu of Song saw the wife of Kong Fu on the road, gazed at her as she passed and watched her leave, saying: "Beautiful and radiant."

【Classic】
Second year, spring, the king's first month, Wushen day, Du of Song murdered his ruler Yiyi and his Grand Master Kong Fu.
○ The Viscount of Teng came to pay homage.
○ In the third month, the Duke met with the Marquis of Qi, the Marquis of Chen, and the Earl of Zheng at Ji, to settle the disorder of Song.
○ Summer, fourth month, took the great tripod of Gao from Song. On Wushen day, it was placed in the Grand Temple.
○ Autumn, seventh month, the Marquis of Qi came to pay homage.
○ The Marquis of Cai and the Earl of Zheng met at Deng.
○ In the ninth month, entered Qi.
○ The Duke swore an alliance with the Rong at Tang. In winter, the Duke returned from Tang.
【Commentary】
Second year, spring, Du of Song attacked the Kong clan, killed Kong Fu, and took his wife. The Duke was angry, and Du, fearing, then murdered Duke Shang. The noble man considered that Du had no respect for his ruler in his heart, and only then acted upon evil, so the text first records the murder of his ruler. They met at Ji to settle the disorder of Song. Because of bribes, they established the Hua clan.
When Duke Shang of Song was established, in ten years there were eleven wars, and the people could not bear the demands. Kong Fujia was Minister of War, and Du was Grand Steward, so because the people could not bear the demands, he first declared: "The Minister of War is the cause." After killing Kong Fu and murdering Duke Shang, he summoned Duke Zhuang from Zheng and established him, to be close to Zheng. He bribed the Duke with the great tripod of Gao, and Qi, Chen, and Zheng all received bribes, so he became chief minister to the Duke of Song.
Summer, fourth month, took the great tripod of Gao from Song. On Wushen day, it was placed in the Grand Temple, which was contrary to ritual. Zang Aibo remonstrated, saying: "A ruler of men will manifest virtue and block wrongdoing, to oversee the hundred officials, still fearing he might fail, so he displays excellent virtue to show his descendants. Therefore the pure temple has a thatched roof, the great carriage has a rush mat, the great sacrifice is not seasoned, and the grain offering is not polished, to manifest frugality. The robes, crown, ceremonial apron, and jade tablet, the belt, lower garment, leggings, and shoes, the headband, cap strings, and chin strap, to manifest regulation. The jade ornaments, scabbard fittings, and knife ornaments, the sash, streamers, and bridle tassels, to manifest rank. The fire, dragon, axe, and ceremonial embroidery patterns, to manifest refinement. The five colors representing images, to manifest things. The bells on the chariot and harness, to manifest sound. The sun, moon, and stars on the flags, to manifest brightness. Virtue is frugal yet regulated, rising and falling according to rank, with patterns and objects to record it, and sounds and brightness to proclaim it, to oversee the hundred officials. The hundred officials thus become cautious and fearful, and dare not violate discipline. Now you have destroyed virtue and established wrongdoing, and placed the vessel of bribery in the Grand Temple, to display it openly to the hundred officials. If the hundred officials imitate it, what punishment can there be? The ruin of a state comes from the corruption of officials; the loss of virtue among officials comes from the prominence of favored bribes. The tripod of Gao in the temple—what prominence could be greater? When King Wu conquered Shang, he moved the nine tripods to Luoyi, and righteous men still criticized him, how much more when one places a vessel of wrongdoing and disorder in the Grand Temple—what can be done about it?" The Duke did not listen.
The Zhou historiographer within heard of this and said: "Zang Sun Da will surely have descendants in Lu! When the ruler errs, he does not forget to remonstrate with virtue."
○ Autumn, seventh month, the Marquis of Qi came to pay homage but was disrespectful. When the Marquis of Qi returned, they planned to attack him.
○ The Marquis of Cai and the Earl of Zheng met at Deng, beginning to fear Chu.
○ In the ninth month, entered Qi, to punish disrespect.
○ The Duke swore an alliance with the Rong at Tang, to restore old friendship. In winter, the Duke returned from Tang and reported at the temple. Whenever the Duke traveled, he reported at the ancestral temple; upon returning, he held a drinking ceremony, set down the cup, and recorded merits—this was ritual. For special meetings, going and coming were recorded by place, to yield to the matter. For meetings of three or more, going was recorded by place, and coming was recorded as a meeting, to complete the matter.
○ Formerly, Lady Jiang, wife of Marquis Mu of Jin, gave birth to the eldest son during the campaign at Tiao, and named him Chou (Enemy). His younger brother was born during the battle at Qianmu, and was named Chengshi (Complete Teacher). Shi Fu said: "How strange, the ruler's naming of his sons! Names regulate righteousness, righteousness produces ritual, ritual embodies governance, and governance corrects the people. Therefore governance succeeds and the people obey; if it changes, disorder arises. A good match is called a consort, a resentful match is called an enemy—this is the ancient naming. Now the ruler names his eldest son Chou and his younger brother Chengshi—this is the first sign of impending disorder. Will the elder brother be replaced?"
In the twenty-fourth year of Hui, Jin began to fall into disorder, so Huan Shu was enfeoffed at Quwo, and Luan Bin, grandson of Marquis Jing, was made his tutor. Shi Fu said: "I have heard that for the establishment of a state, the root must be great and the branches small, and only then can it be secure. Therefore the Son of Heaven establishes states, the feudal lords establish houses, the ministers establish concubines, the grand masters have secondary clans, the officers have retainers and sons, and the common people, artisans, and merchants each have their own kin, all with gradations of rank. Therefore the people serve their superiors, and those below have no covetous ambitions. Now Jin is a marquisate within the royal domain, yet a state has been established—the root is already weakened; can it last long?"
In the thirtieth year of Hui, Pan Fu of Jin murdered Marquis Zhao and tried to install Huan Shu, but failed. The people of Jin established Marquis Xiao. In the forty-fifth year of Hui, Zhuang Bo of Quwo attacked Yi and murdered Marquis Xiao. The people of Yi established his younger brother, Marquis E. Marquis E fathered Marquis Ai. Marquis Ai encroached upon the fields of Xingting. The southern border of Xingting incited Quwo to attack Yi.

自唐以来，百姓对狼的印象已基本趋向于负面的意义，北方的蛮夷时叩边关，他们带来的狼头标志，致使中原百姓将狼和凶狠贪婪联系到了一起。唐宋诗人多有讽刺仇视北方突厥、辽人的作品，他们以狼喻胡，多加贬词，自然与胡人自认狼种颇有关联。
en:
Weapons carved like halberds bore leopard tails, and crimson banners were adorned with wolf heads. 

Since the Tang Dynasty, the public impression of wolves had become increasingly negative. When northern nomadic tribes invaded the frontiers, they brought banners with wolf head symbols, which led Central Plains' Commoners to associate wolves with ferocity and greed.Poets of the Tang and Song dynasties often wrote satirical works criticizing the Turkics and Khitans, using wolves as metaphors for these groups, laden with contempt. This naturally stemmed from the nomads' own self-identification as "descendants of wolves."

zh:
【下经·䷞】

䷞
咸：亨，利贞，取女吉。
彖曰：咸，感也。柔上而刚下，二气感应以相与。止而说，男下女，是以“亨，利贞，取女吉”也。天地感而万物化生，圣人感人心而天下和平。观其所感，而天地万物之情可见矣。
《象》曰：山上有泽，咸。君子以虚受人。
初六：咸其拇。
《象》曰：“咸其拇”，志在外也。
六二：咸其腓，凶，居吉。
《象》曰：虽“凶居吉”，顺不害也。
九三：咸其股，执其随，往吝。
《象》曰：“咸其股”，亦不处也。志在随人，所执下也。
九四：贞吉，悔亡。憧憧往来，朋从尔思。
《象》曰：“贞吉悔亡”，未感害也。“憧憧往来”，未光大也。
九五：咸其脢，无悔。
《象》曰：“咸其脢”，志末也。
上六：咸其辅颊舌。
《象》曰：“咸其辅颊舌”，滕口说也。
en:
【Lower Canon·䷞】

䷞
Xian (Influence): Success. Favorable to be steadfast and upright. Taking a maiden to wife brings good fortune.
The Commentary on the Judgment says: Xian means influence. The soft (yin) is above and the firm (yang) is below; the two vital forces respond to and unite with each other. Restraint with joy, the Type Ⅰ humbles himself before the Type Ⅱ. Therefore, "Success. Favorable to be steadfast and upright. Taking a maiden to wife brings good fortune." Heaven and Earth influence each other, and all things are transformed and born. The Emperor influences the hearts of the people, and the world is at peace. Observing what is influenced, the true nature of Heaven, Earth, and all things can be seen.
The Image says: A lake rests on the Mountain. This is Xian (Influence). The noble one, through emptiness, receives others.
Initial Six: Influencing the big toe.
The Image says: "Influencing the big toe" means the will is directed outward.
Second Six: Influencing the calf. Inauspicious. Remaining still brings good fortune.
The Image says: Although "Inauspicious, remaining still brings good fortune," yielding does not bring harm.
Third Nine: Influencing the thigh, holding to what it follows. To advance brings regret.
The Image says: "Influencing the thigh" also means not staying in place. The will is to follow others, and what it holds to is lowly.
Fourth Nine: Steadfastness brings good fortune; regrets disappear. Restless comings and goings; friends will follow your Wisdom.
The Image says: "Steadfastness brings good fortune; regrets disappear" means it has not yet been harmed by influence. "Restless comings and goings" means it is not yet great and bright.
Fifth Nine: Influencing the back. No Regrets.
The Image says: "Influencing the back" means the will is on the insignificant.
Top Six: Influencing the jaws, cheeks, and tongue.
The Image says: "Influencing the jaws, cheeks, and tongue" means speaking with glib words.
Gao Lingyun

zh:
【问丧第三十五】

亲始死，鸡斯徒跣，扱上衽，交手哭。恻怛之心，痛疾之意，伤肾干肝焦肺，水浆不入口，三日不举火，故邻里为之糜粥以饮食之。夫悲哀在中，故形变于外也，痛疾在心，故口不甘味，身不安美也。
三日而敛，在床曰尸，在棺曰柩，动尸举柩，哭踊无数。恻怛之心，痛疾之意，悲哀志懑气盛，故袒而踊之，所以动体安心下气也。妇人不宜袒，故发胸击心爵踊，殷殷田田，如坏墙然，悲哀痛疾之至也。故曰：“辟踊哭泣，哀以送之。送形而往，迎精而反也。”
其往送也，望望然、汲汲然如有追而弗及也；其反哭也，皇皇然若有求而弗得也。故其往送也如慕，其反也如疑。
求而无所得之也，入门而弗见也，上堂又弗见也，入室又弗见也。亡矣丧矣！不可复见矣！故哭泣辟踊，尽哀而止矣。心怅焉怆焉、惚焉忾焉，心绝志悲而已矣。祭之宗庙，以鬼飨之，徼幸复反也。
成圹而归，不敢入处室，居于倚庐，哀亲之在外也；寝苫枕块，哀亲之在土也。故哭泣无时，服勤三年，思慕之心，孝子之志也，人情之实也。
或问曰：“死三日而后敛者，何也？”曰：孝子亲死，悲哀志懑，故匍匐而哭之，若将复生然，安可得夺而敛之也。故曰三日而后敛者，以俟其生也；三日而不生，亦不生矣。孝子之心亦益衰矣；家室之计，衣服之具，亦可以成矣；亲戚之远者，亦可以至矣。是故圣人为之断决以三日为之礼制也。
或问曰：“冠者不肉袒，何也？”曰：冠，至尊也，不居肉袒之体也，故为之免以代之也。
然则秃者不免，伛者不袒，跛者不踊，非不悲也；身有锢疾，不可以备礼也。故曰：丧礼唯哀为主矣。女子哭泣悲哀，击胸伤心；男子哭泣悲哀，稽颡触地无容，哀之至也。
或问曰：“免者以何为也？”曰：不冠者之所服也。《礼》曰：“童子不缌，唯当室缌。”缌者其免也，当室则免而杖矣。
或问曰：“杖者何也？”曰：竹、桐一也。故为父苴杖--苴杖，竹也；为母削杖--削杖，桐也。
……
en:
【Questions on Mourning Rituals, Part 35】

When a parent first dies, the mourner lets down his hair, bares his feet, tucks up the hem of his garment, and beats his breast while weeping. The grief in his heart, the anguish of his sorrow, wounds his kidneys, parches his liver, and sears his lungs. No water or gruel passes his lips, and for three days no fire is lit in his home. Thus neighbors prepare porridge and drink to sustain him. When sorrow dwells within, the body transforms without; when anguish fills the heart, the mouth loses taste for food, and the body finds no comfort in fine attire.
After three days, the body is encoffined. On the bed it is called a corpse; in the coffin it is called a bier. When moving the corpse or lifting the bier, weeping and leaping know no limit. The grief in his heart, the anguish of his sorrow, the sorrow and frustration swelling within—therefore he bares his arm and leaps, to stir his body, calm his heart, and ease his breath. Women, not suited to baring their arms, instead expose their chests, beat their breasts, and leap like pheasants, with sounds like crumbling walls—such is the extremity of grief and anguish. Thus it is said: "Beating the breast and leaping, weeping and wailing, send off the dead with sorrow. Escorting the form away, one welcomes back the spirit."
When going forth to see the dead off, he gazes ahead anxiously, urgently, as if pursuing something he cannot catch; when returning to weep, he is distraught, as if seeking something he cannot find. Thus his going forth is like longing, and his return is like doubt.
He seeks but finds nothing; he enters the gate and does not see them, ascends the hall and does not see them, enters the chamber and does not see them. Gone! Lost! Never to be seen again! Therefore he weeps and wails, beats his breast and leaps, until his grief is spent and he stops. His heart is desolate, mournful, dazed, and sighing—his spirit is broken and his will is sorrowful, and that is all. He offers sacrifices in the ancestral temple, presenting offerings to the ghost, hoping against hope that the deceased might return.
After the tomb is sealed and he returns home, he dares not enter his inner chambers but dwells in a lean-to hut, grieving that his parent lies outside; he sleeps on straw with a clod of earth for a pillow, grieving that his parent is in the ground. Thus he weeps without set times, and serves the mourning duties for three years. The heart of longing and remembrance is the will of a filial son, the true expression of human feeling.
Someone asks: "Why is the body encoffined only after three days?" The answer: When a filial son's parent dies, his sorrow and frustration overwhelm him, so he crawls and weeps over the body, as if the parent might come back to life—how could he bear to be deprived of this and have the body encoffined? Thus it is said: the encoffining is delayed three days to wait for the parent to revive; if after three days the parent does not revive, then there is no revival. The filial son's hope also gradually fades; the household's preparations and the grave clothes can now be completed; distant relatives can now arrive. Therefore the sages established the rule of three days as the ritual standard.
Someone asks: "Why do those wearing a cap not bare their arms?" The answer: The cap is most honorable and does not rest upon a bared body, so the mourning cap is worn in its place.
Yet the bald need not wear the mourning cap, the hunchbacked need not bare their arms, and the lame need not leap—not because they lack sorrow, but because their bodies have chronic afflictions that prevent full ritual observance. Thus it is said: In mourning rites, sorrow alone is paramount. Women weep in grief, beating their breasts in anguish; men weep in grief, knocking their foreheads to the ground without restraint—such is the extremity of sorrow.
Someone asks: "What is the mourning cap for?" The answer: It is worn by those who do not wear the formal cap. The Rites say: "A youth does not wear the coarse mourning sash, except when he heads a household; then he wears it." The sash accompanies the mourning cap; when one heads a household, he wears the cap and uses the staff.
Someone asks: "What is the staff for?" The answer: Bamboo and tung wood serve the same purpose. Thus for the father one uses a rough staff—the rough staff is of bamboo; for the mother one uses a smoothed staff—the smoothed staff is of tung wood.

zh:
【周书·泰誓上】

惟十有一年，武王伐殷。一月戊午，师渡孟津，作泰誓三篇。泰誓：
惟十有三年春，大会于孟津。
王曰：“嗟！我友邦冢君，越我御事庶士，明听誓。惟天地万物父母，惟人万物之灵。亶聪明，作元后，元后作民父母。
“今商王受，弗敬上天，降灾下民，沈湎冒色，敢行暴虐，罪人以族，官人以世，惟宫室台榭陂池侈服，以残害于尔万姓。焚炙忠良，刳剔孕妇。皇天震怒，命我文考，肃将天威，大勋未集。肆予小子发，以尔友邦冢君，观政于商。惟受罔有悛心，乃夷居，弗事上帝神祇，遗厥先宗庙弗祀，牺牲粢盛既于凶盗。乃曰：‘吾有民有命！’罔惩其侮。
“天佑下民，作之君，作之师。惟其克相上帝，宠绥四方。有罪无罪，予曷敢有越厥志？同力度德，同德度义。受有臣亿万，惟亿万心；予有臣三千，惟一心。商罪贯盈，天命诛之。予弗顺天，厥罪惟钧。
“予小子夙夜祗惧，受命文考，类于上帝，宜于冢土，以尔有众，砥天之罚。天矜于民，民之所欲，天必从之。尔尚弼予一人，永清四海，时哉弗可失！”
en:
[The Book of Zhou: The Great Oath, Part I]

In the 11th year, King Wu attacked Yin. In the first month, on the day Wuwu, the army crossed at Mengjin, and he made the Great Oath in three parts. The Great Oath:
On the 13th year (B.C. 1121,) in the spring, there was a great assembly (of the barons) at Mengjin.
When the king said, Oh! my friendly states, and high captains! it has fallen to me to manage these affairs, do all of you warriors, therefore, attentively listen to this my oath. Heaven and earth are the parents of all things. People are the most intelligent part of sublunary things; the most truly intellectual of people become chief rulers, and the chief ruler is the parent of the people.
Now Shou, the ruler of Shang, has been disrespectful towards high Heaven, and thus brought down calamities upon these lower people. Immersed in wine, and disordered by lust, he dared to practice tyranny and oppression; offenders were made to involve their relatives, and offices were rendered hereditary in families, while he only thought of palaces and buildings, terraces and groves, dikes and pools, with extravagant apparel, to the injury and ruin of you all people. At the same time he burned and roasted the faithful and honest, flaying and ripping open pregnant women; so that high Heaven became incensed, and ordered my accomplished predecessor (Wen-wang) reverently to sustain the celestial dignity; but while his great merit was still incomplete, (he died.) Therefore I, the insignificant one, by the reverting to me of you friendly estates and high captains, have shewn the tendency of his government over the Shang dynasty; Shou (the tyrant) has not the slightest disposition to reform; but on the contrary he sits on his heels, and refuses to serve the Supreme Ruler, with the celestial and terrestrial gods; neglecting the temple of his ancestors without sacrificing to them; while the sacrificial oil and meat-offerings are given over to be consumed by ruffians and robbers; at the same time he exclaims, 'I have the people, and the decree is with me,' and all without reproving his insolence.
Heaven out of compassion to the inferior people has appointed over them princes, and given them instructors, that they may be able to assist the Supreme in cherishing and tranquillizing the four quarters (of the world). Thus with regard to the guilty or the innocent, how dare we transgress his will! When the strength (of contending parties) is equal, let us measure each other's virtue; should virtue be equal let us estimate the justice (of our respective claims.) Shou, (the tyrant) has thousands and millions of servants, and thousands and millions of minds. I have only three thousand followers, but they are all of one mind. Shang's crimes are pervading and overflowing, so that Heaven has given command to destroy him; if I do not obey (the will of) Heaven, my guilt will be equal to his.
I, the insignificant one, day and night tremble with apprehension; having received the decree from my accomplished predecessor, I have sacrificed to the Supreme Ruler and made offerings to the gods of the land and grain; and now with you multitudes, I will carry out the inflictions of Heaven. When Heaven shows compassion towards the people, which the people desire heaven will grant it to them; do you therefore assist me, a single individual, lastingly cleanse (all within) the four seas; this is now the time, and the opportunity must not be lost.

The child was too young to know what to do with the fish, so he cleaned and prepared it himself. For the first time, his sword was used to save a life, not take one.

其中虽有遵循传统礼节的缘故，但也不乏万一对方心意有变，经过媒人也好斡旋，留些颜面的意思。

An aged marriage proposal card. It has been around for some years, and the birth dates and names are no longer legible.
According to marital customs, this should have been written and delivered by a matchmaker to perform the "Inquiring the Name" step of the Six Traditional Rites.
Following this tradition is partly about etiquette, but also serves to save face: if the other party has a change of heart, the matchmaker can mediate the rejection gracefully.
However, the gentleman who wrote this card was far too eager and penned it himself, only to be caught in the act by his beloved.
Thus, he was rejected. Alas! Those who know the tale can only pity him.
